CrownX anti-forensic recovery/artifact destruction (VSS + Prefetch/AmCache/SRUM/BAM + PhysicalDrive) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts CrownX's recovery-inhibition and anti-forensic subsystem: deletion of Windows forensic stores (Prefetch, AmCache, SRUM, BAM/DAM, PowerShell history), WinRE/System-Restore wiping, and direct \\.\PhysicalDrive raw-disk access. Distinct from a generic vssadmin rule by pivoting on the forensic-store/raw-disk targets Blackpoint enumerated. Rationale: Blackpoint explicitly lists CrownX's anti-forensic targets: VSS, WinRE, System Restore, Prefetch, AmCache, SRUM, BAM, DAM, ShimCache, PowerShell history, and \\.\PhysicalDrive%d direct disk access. Deleting these forensic stores in a tight burst (plus raw-disk/reagentc/vssadmin signals) is a strong ransomware-impact indicator that a lone vssadmin rule misses. Sigma skipped: this UC is a threshold + cross-signal correlation, not single-event shape. Corroborated Blackpoint blog. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/avalons-path-from-legal-lure-to-crownx-ransom-capabilities/
ATT&CKT1490 T1070.004 T1561.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Disk-cleanup / privacy tools (CCleaner, BleachBit) purging Prefetch and PowerShell history
  • SysAdmin running reagentc /disable during WinRE servicing or imaging
  • Legit ransomware-hardening scripts that pre-emptively clear SRUM/BAM during forensic-readiness testing
  • Backup software pruning VSS snapshots as part of retention
  • OS reset / re-imaging workflow that wipes Amcache/Prefetch
Suppression filter
| where Actor !in~ ("ccleaner.exe","bleachbit.exe","cleanmgr.exe","dism.exe") and Actor !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process doing the burst deletions (InitiatingProcessId/ContextImageFileName) and whether \\.\PhysicalDrive or reagentc /disable co-occurred on the host; correlate to any .8hn2yc writes. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately (raw-disk access can brick boot records), suspend the actor account, and snapshot/preserve any remaining VSS from a hypervisor level if virtual. 3) Hunt: check for the MSBuild loader chain and helloxcherry.com C2 on the same host, and sweep backup/virtualization assets (Veeam/Acronis/vCenter/Hyper-V) for the same deletion pattern indicating recovery-platform targeting.
let ForensicDeletes = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ActionType == "FileDeleted"
    | where FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\Prefetch\", @"\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve", @"\System32\sru\", @"\System32\LogFiles\Sum\", "ConsoleHost_history.txt")
    | summarize DeleteCount = count(), Targets = make_set(FolderPath, 20), Actor = any(InitiatingProcessFileName)
              by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
    | where DeleteCount > 3;
let RawDiskOrRecovery = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has @"\\.\PhysicalDrive"
        or (FileName =~ "reagentc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "disable")
        or (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "delete shadows")
        or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RawSignal = ProcessCommandLine, Actor2 = InitiatingProcessFileName;
ForensicDeletes
| join kind=leftouter (RawDiskOrRecovery | summarize RawSignals = make_set(RawSignal, 10) by DeviceName) on DeviceName
| project DeviceName, Timestamp, DeleteCount, Targets, Actor, RawSignals
| order by DeleteCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "FileDeleted"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Windows\Prefetch\", @"\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve", @"\System32\sru\", @"\System32\LogFiles\Sum\", "ConsoleHost_history.txt")
| summarize DeleteCount = count(), Targets = make_set(TargetFilePath, 20), Actor = any(ActingProcessName)
          by DvcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DeleteCount > 3
| order by DeleteCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @EventType:(Delete OR DeletedExecutable) @TargetFilename:(*\\Windows\\Prefetch\\* OR *\\Amcache.hve* OR *\\System32\\sru\\* OR *ConsoleHost_history.txt*)
#event_simpleName=FileDeleted TargetFileName=/(\\Windows\\Prefetch\\|Amcache\.hve|\\System32\\sru\\|ConsoleHost_history\.txt)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=DeleteCount))
| DeleteCount > 3

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b7d50d0406afcd2efd87bf3bf8c4211719ba9817dd2e0ad62af10c933e765e28", "607cb58b8a592885eef5cfbe35ddce962741b0775c575f58cb3a96ca0ee893a6", "59a260716d05c20229c6a46fe0a2fb5b80fa30c9c73a850222d9d3454426a60a", "4b7301f02b8312ae6de614981f325dbbabee32166630618fdff74615d9a487ba", "c725815cbb07ab5be8903e74ef8aea46ef9c25e4a3bc626ae94bfc1ae21df6e3") or SHA1 in~ ("b7d50d0406afcd2efd87bf3bf8c4211719ba9817dd2e0ad62af10c933e765e28", "607cb58b8a592885eef5cfbe35ddce962741b0775c575f58cb3a96ca0ee893a6", "59a260716d05c20229c6a46fe0a2fb5b80fa30c9c73a850222d9d3454426a60a", "4b7301f02b8312ae6de614981f325dbbabee32166630618fdff74615d9a487ba", "c725815cbb07ab5be8903e74ef8aea46ef9c25e4a3bc626ae94bfc1ae21df6e3") or MD5 in~ ("b7d50d0406afcd2efd87bf3bf8c4211719ba9817dd2e0ad62af10c933e765e28", "607cb58b8a592885eef5cfbe35ddce962741b0775c575f58cb3a96ca0ee893a6", "59a260716d05c20229c6a46fe0a2fb5b80fa30c9c73a850222d9d3454426a60a", "4b7301f02b8312ae6de614981f325dbbabee32166630618fdff74615d9a487ba", "c725815cbb07ab5be8903e74ef8aea46ef9c25e4a3bc626ae94bfc1ae21df6e3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b7d50d0406afcd2efd87bf3bf8c4211719ba9817dd2e0ad62af10c933e765e28", "607cb58b8a592885eef5cfbe35ddce962741b0775c575f58cb3a96ca0ee893a6", "59a260716d05c20229c6a46fe0a2fb5b80fa30c9c73a850222d9d3454426a60a", "4b7301f02b8312ae6de614981f325dbbabee32166630618fdff74615d9a487ba", "c725815cbb07ab5be8903e74ef8aea46ef9c25e4a3bc626ae94bfc1ae21df6e3") or SHA1 in~ ("b7d50d0406afcd2efd87bf3bf8c4211719ba9817dd2e0ad62af10c933e765e28", "607cb58b8a592885eef5cfbe35ddce962741b0775c575f58cb3a96ca0ee893a6", "59a260716d05c20229c6a46fe0a2fb5b80fa30c9c73a850222d9d3454426a60a", "4b7301f02b8312ae6de614981f325dbbabee32166630618fdff74615d9a487ba", "c725815cbb07ab5be8903e74ef8aea46ef9c25e4a3bc626ae94bfc1ae21df6e3") or MD5 in~ ("b7d50d0406afcd2efd87bf3bf8c4211719ba9817dd2e0ad62af10c933e765e28", "607cb58b8a592885eef5cfbe35ddce962741b0775c575f58cb3a96ca0ee893a6", "59a260716d05c20229c6a46fe0a2fb5b80fa30c9c73a850222d9d3454426a60a", "4b7301f02b8312ae6de614981f325dbbabee32166630618fdff74615d9a487ba", "c725815cbb07ab5be8903e74ef8aea46ef9c25e4a3bc626ae94bfc1ae21df6e3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b7d50d0406afcd2efd87bf3bf8c4211719ba9817dd2e0ad62af10c933e765e28", "607cb58b8a592885eef5cfbe35ddce962741b0775c575f58cb3a96ca0ee893a6", "59a260716d05c20229c6a46fe0a2fb5b80fa30c9c73a850222d9d3454426a60a", "4b7301f02b8312ae6de614981f325dbbabee32166630618fdff74615d9a487ba", "c725815cbb07ab5be8903e74ef8aea46ef9c25e4a3bc626ae94bfc1ae21df6e3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

North Korea-Linked npm Packages Mimic Rollup Polyfills to Steal Developer Secrets

The Hacker News
2026-07-03 15 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors with ties to North Korea have been linked to a fresh set of malicious npm packages that masquerade as Rollup polyfill tooling to facilitate remote access and data theft. According to JFrog, the packages "rollup-packages-polyfill-core" and "rollup-runtime-polyfill-core" mimic the legitimate "rollup-plugin-polyfill-node" project, down to the description, repository metadata, and

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Lazarus rollup-polyfill lookalike npm packages installed into node_modules · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] npm/node egress to Lazarus rollup-polyfill C2 216.126.236.244 · [LLM] node.exe resolving jsonkeeper.com dead-drop resolver · [LLM] security-alerts-sdk PyPI backdoor beacon to 142.93.211.30:5000 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] node.exe bulk-reading developer, cloud & AI-tool secrets (rollup-polyfill collector) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Lazarus rollup-polyfill lookalike npm packages installed into node_modules AIDelivery High
Hunts creation of the six named malicious npm packages (and the @nut-tree-fork/nut-js RAT dependency) under node_modules on developer workstations and CI build agents. Article-specific because it keys on the exact package names JFrog attributed to this North Korea-linked campaign, not generic postinstall behaviour. Rationale: Uses the six exact package names JFrog published (rollup-packages-polyfill-core, rollup-runtime-polyfill-core, rollup-plugin-polyfill-connect, swift-parse-stream, quirky-token, react-icon-svgs) plus the @nut-tree-fork/nut-js input-control dependency, anchored to node_modules so folder-name collisions are ruled out. Named IOCs give near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/rollup-polyfill-masquerading/ • https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319672/20260704/north-koreas-lazarus-group-hid-full-rat-six-rollup-polyfill-npm-packages.htm
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware researcher intentionally installing the package in an analysis VM
  • Threat-intel enrichment sandbox pulling the sample from an npm mirror
  • Internal npm proxy/mirror caching the (now-removed) package for retro-hunt
  • A developer restoring an old lockfile that still pins the malicious version
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\malware-analysis\\" and DeviceName !startswith "SANDBOX-"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the write host is a real dev/CI endpoint (not a sanctioned malware lab); pull the installing process tree (npm/node) and the initiating user. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, delete the node_modules tree, and treat every credential reachable from it (npm tokens, SSH/AWS/Azure keys, git creds) as compromised — force rotation. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host/user for outbound to 216.126.236.244 and jsonkeeper.com, and search other build agents/lockfiles for the same package names.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where FolderPath has_any ("rollup-packages-polyfill-core","rollup-runtime-polyfill-core","rollup-plugin-polyfill-connect","swift-parse-stream","quirky-token","react-icon-svgs","nut-js")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("rollup-packages-polyfill-core","rollup-runtime-polyfill-core","rollup-plugin-polyfill-connect","swift-parse-stream","quirky-token","react-icon-svgs","nut-js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/node egress to Lazarus rollup-polyfill C2 216.126.236.244 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host contacting 216.126.236.244, the server the decrypted JSONKeeper stage reaches out to for the encrypted JavaScript RAT payload in the JFrog campaign. Article-specific because it keys on the exact campaign C2 IP. Rationale: 216.126.236.244 is the concrete second-stage payload host named by JFrog and re-reported by TechTimes; any endpoint reaching it is high-confidence compromise regardless of the initiating binary. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/rollup-polyfill-masquerading/ • https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319672/20260704/north-koreas-lazarus-group-hid-full-rat-six-rollup-polyfill-npm-packages.htm
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform/proxy actively validating the IOC
  • Malware sandbox detonating the sample and beaconing out
  • Shared-hosting IP later reassigned to a benign service (validate WHOIS/timeline before closing)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process (expect node.exe) and whether it followed a jsonkeeper.com fetch; grab the payload if EDR captured it. 2) CONTAIN: Block 216.126.236.244 at egress/firewall, isolate the host, and rotate all developer secrets on it. 3) HUNT: Sweep all hosts for the six malicious npm packages and for jsonkeeper.com resolutions preceding this beacon.

| order by TimeGenerated desc

node.exe resolving jsonkeeper.com dead-drop resolver AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts node/npm processes resolving or connecting to jsonkeeper.com, the JSONKeeper URL the second-stage SVG-lookalike packages fetch and eval the model field from. Scoping the initiator to node prevents FPs from legitimate ad-hoc JSONKeeper usage. Rationale: jsonkeeper.com is the specific dead-drop resolver JFrog documented for the second-stage 'fetch JSON and eval model field' behaviour; requiring node.exe/npm as the initiator turns an otherwise generic domain into a build-context anomaly. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/rollup-polyfill-masquerading/
ATT&CKT1102 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately using JSONKeeper as a quick JSON store in a Node prototype
  • Node-based test suites hitting jsonkeeper.com fixtures
  • Security researcher replaying the sample
  • Third-party npm tooling that happens to use JSONKeeper for config
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve the full node command line / script path and confirm it correlates with one of the malicious packages in node_modules. 2) CONTAIN: If confirmed, isolate host, block jsonkeeper.com egress for build hosts, and rotate dev secrets. 3) HUNT: Follow the chain to 216.126.236.244 beacons and check other CI agents for the same DNS + package footprint.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "jsonkeeper.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node","npm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "jsonkeeper.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

node.exe bulk-reading developer, cloud & AI-tool secrets (rollup-polyfill collector) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the file-collection stage: a node.exe process reading multiple distinct credential/AI-tool config artifacts (.aws/.ssh/.npmrc, Cursor/Windsurf/VS Code history, Google Gemini/Anthropic Claude/Foundry configs). Article-specific in its targeting of AI-coding-tool history and configs, which JFrog called out explicitly. Expressed on read-capable EDR telemetry (Falcon FileOpenInfo / CIM Filesystem read); Windows-native tables lack file-read events. Rationale: The collector's targeting of Cursor/Windsurf/VS Code editor history plus Gemini/Claude/Foundry AI-tool configs alongside .aws/.ssh/.npmrc is the campaign's signature (per JFrog); requiring a node.exe reader touching >=3 distinct secret files keeps it behavioural. Left Defender/Sentinel/Datadog empty because Windows EDR/Sysmon do not emit file-read events - only read-capable EDR (Falcon FileOpenInfo) or CIM Filesystem read populates this. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/rollup-polyfill-masquerading/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node-based dev tool legitimately reading ~/.npmrc and ~/.aws for build config
  • VS Code/Cursor extensions written in Node indexing editor history
  • Backup/sync agent implemented in Node walking the home directory
  • Credential-scanner/secret-linter tooling run by the developer
Suppression filter
| search NOT (Filesystem.process_path="*\\Microsoft VS Code\\*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*\\Cursor\\resources\\*")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Get the node script path/command line and confirm it maps to a suspicious package (not a known IDE extension); list which secret files were read. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host and rotate every credential in the accessed files (AWS/Azure/Gemini/Claude keys, SSH keys, npm tokens). 3) HUNT: Correlate with 216.126.236.244 / jsonkeeper.com egress and check whether @nut-tree-fork/nut-js was installed (remote-control capability).

security-alerts-sdk PyPI backdoor beacon to 142.93.211.30:5000 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the polling backdoor in the trojanized 'security-alerts-sdk' PyPI package periodically contacting 142.93.211.30 on TCP/5000 to fetch commands and exfiltrate SSH/AWS/Docker/npm/PyPI/git secrets. Article-specific to the exact C2 IP:port pair. Rationale: 142.93.211.30:5000 is the concrete polling C2 the article attributes to security-alerts-sdk (SafeDep-tracked cluster); the exact IP+port pair makes any hit high-confidence with minimal FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/north-korea-linked-npm-packages-mimic.html • https://safedep.io/ti/campaigns/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1059.006
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign service later hosted on the DigitalOcean IP 142.93.211.30 (validate timeline)
  • Internal port-5000 dev service coincidentally sharing the IP string in a NAT log
  • Security researcher detonating security-alerts-sdk in a lab
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the initiating process is python and check site-packages for 'security-alerts-sdk'; capture the beacon cadence. 2) CONTAIN: Block 142.93.211.30, isolate host, uninstall the package, and rotate SSH keys, AWS creds, Docker/npm/PyPI/git tokens and .env secrets it can read. 3) HUNT: Search all hosts for pip installs of security-alerts-sdk and for the same C2 IP across network logs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "142.93.211.30" and RemotePort == 5000
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "142.93.211.30" and DstPortNumber == 5000
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"

| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

          NewProcessName, CommandLine

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Armored Likho Targets Government Agencies, Power Sector with BusySnake Stealer

The Hacker News
2026-07-03 22 use cases 9 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A previously undocumented threat actor known as Armored Likho has been attributed to cyber attacks targeting government agencies and the electric power sector across Russia, Brazil, and Kazakhstan. "Armored Likho blends financially motivated campaigns targeting private individuals with targeted cyber espionage aimed at organizations," Kaspersky said in a technical analysis published today. "

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Armored Likho dropper writes twin VBScript files (trace-eraser + scheduled-task launcher) from archive extract dir · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2025-9491 LNK exploitation: Explorer spawns obfuscated PowerShell loader + decoy document · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BusySnake persistence: VBScript (wscript/cscript) registers scheduled task launching pythonw/.pyw stealer · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BusySnake C2 beacon to Armored Likho infrastructure (named domains + IPs) · [LLM] BusySnake deploys remote-access tooling: Python stealer spawns RustDesk / Go2Tunnel reverse SSH tunnel · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] BusySnake credential collection: pythonw stages browser cred stores, Telegram session, and crypto-wallet JSON · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Armored Likho dropper writes twin VBScript files (trace-eraser + scheduled-task launcher) from archive extract dir AIDelivery High
Hunts the BusySnake delivery EXE that, after extraction from a spear-phished RAR, drops TWO VBScript files on the same host in one burst — one to erase execution traces, one to register the stealer via a scheduled task. The dual-.vbs-from-one-EXE-in-a-user-temp-path pattern is the article's specific dropper fingerprint. Rationale: Article states the dropper 'creates two VBScript (VBScript) files that are responsible for erasing traces of the initial execution as well as launching the stealer by means of a scheduled task' — the count>=2 twin-.vbs-from-one-EXE constraint is what separates this from benign single-script installers. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/armored-likho-apt-with-busysnake-stealer/120292/ • https://www.securityweek.com/armored-likho-apt-targeting-government-electric-power-entities/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1070.004 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers (e.g. some VPN/printer setups) that drop helper .vbs files to Temp
  • Admin logon-script packaging tools writing multiple .vbs to a staging folder
  • SCCM/Intune app-deployment wrappers extracting VBS-based custom actions
  • Backup or migration utilities that generate paired .vbs helper scripts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe","install.exe","ccmsetup.exe","msiexec.exe","vc_redist.x64.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\ccmcache\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessSHA256 and check it against the article MD5s (e.g. 5D5C3E483C5E544260CE98FC29FBF192); inspect both .vbs bodies — one should call schtasks/Schedule.Service, the other del/erase of the parent. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the dropper EXE, remove the registered scheduled task and quarantine both .vbs plus the parent archive. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same EXE hash org-wide, look for subsequent pythonw.exe/.pyw execution and outbound connections to the BusySnake C2 domains/IPs on the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".vbs"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Public\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize VbsCount = dcount(FolderPath), Files = make_set(FileName, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where VbsCount >= 2   // dropper drops BOTH the trace-eraser AND the scheduled-task launcher .vbs
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".vbs"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Public\")
| where ActingProcessName endswith ".exe"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize VbsCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), Files = make_set(TargetFileName, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| where VbsCount >= 2   // twin .vbs drop from a single EXE = BusySnake dropper signature
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*.vbs OR *.VBS) @Image:(*\Temp\* OR *\temp\* OR *\Downloads\* OR *\AppData\*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\.vbs$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(Temp|Downloads|AppData)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=VbsCount))
| VbsCount >= 2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(Filesystem.file_path) as vbs_paths values(Filesystem.file_name) as vbs_files min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" (Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\Roaming\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Public\\*") Filesystem.process_name="*.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where vbs_paths>=2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Filesystem.file_path) as vbs_paths values(Filesystem.file_name) as vbs_files min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" (Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\Roaming\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Public\\*") Filesystem.process_name="*.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where vbs_paths>=2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
CVE-2025-9491 LNK exploitation: Explorer spawns obfuscated PowerShell loader + decoy document AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the alternate BusySnake chain where a weaponized .lnk abuses CVE-2025-9491 (whitespace-padded LNK arguments) so that double-clicking it makes explorer.exe launch an obfuscated PowerShell command that stages the Python stealer while showing a decoy doc. Pivot is the explorer.exe→powershell parent/child with hidden-window + inline-download tokens, distinct from generic encoded-PS alerts by the LNK launch vector. Rationale: Article: the LNK chain 'is abused to trigger the execution of an obfuscated PowerShell command that launches a loader responsible for displaying a decoy document, while preparing the environment for the execution of the Python stealer.' Explorer as the direct parent captures the LNK-double-click vector for CVE-2025-9491. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/armored-likho-apt-with-busysnake-stealer/120292/ • https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/advisories/ZDI-25-148/ • https://www.theregister.com/2025/12/04/microsoft_lnk_bug_fix
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin desktop-shortcut launchers that legitimately call PowerShell with DownloadFile for internal tooling
  • IT self-service .lnk that runs a signed PowerShell installer from an intranet share
  • RMM/monitoring agents shipping shortcuts that invoke PowerShell with -enc
  • Developer shortcuts using IEX against internal package feeds
Suppression filter
| where not (Cmd has_any ("intranet","\\\\corp\\") and SHA256 in (dynamic([])))
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the full PowerShell command line and the parent .lnk (Prefetch / RecentDocs / the folder Explorer opened from) — confirm whitespace-padded arguments and any URL/decoy path. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the PowerShell + any child pythonw.exe, and quarantine the .lnk and staged loader. 3) Hunt: check DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for CVE-2025-9491 exposure across the fleet and search for the same decoy filename or download URL on other hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend Cmd = tolower(ProcessCommandLine)
| where Cmd has_any ("hidden","-enc","-e ","frombase64string","downloadstring","downloadfile","iex","invoke-expression")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "pwsh.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend Cmd = tolower(CommandLine)
| where Cmd has_any ("hidden","-enc","-e ","frombase64string","downloadstring","downloadfile","iex","invoke-expression")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: CVE-2025-9491 LNK Explorer-Spawned Obfuscated PowerShell Loader
id: 8f2a1c4e-7b93-4d21-9a6e-3c5f0b1d2e77
description: Explorer.exe spawning PowerShell with hidden-window and inline-download tokens, consistent with CVE-2025-9491 weaponized LNK execution used by Armored Likho
references:
  - https://securelist.com/tr/armored-likho-apt-with-busysnake-stealer/120292/
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-9491

  - attack.t1204.002

  obfusc:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'hidden'
      - '-enc'
      - 'FromBase64String'
      - 'DownloadString'
      - 'DownloadFile'
      - 'IEX'
      - 'Invoke-Expression'
  condition: selection and obfusc
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\explorer.exe OR *\Explorer.EXE) @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe) @CommandLine:(*hidden* OR *Hidden* OR *-enc* OR *FromBase64String* OR *DownloadString* OR *DownloadFile* OR *IEX* OR *Invoke-Expression*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/explorer\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(hidden|-enc|FromBase64String|DownloadString|DownloadFile|IEX|Invoke-Expression)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name=explorer.exe (Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe) (Processes.process="*hidden*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*" OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadFile*" OR Processes.process="*IEX*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name=explorer.exe (Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe) (Processes.process="*hidden*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*" OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadFile*" OR Processes.process="*IEX*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
BusySnake persistence: VBScript (wscript/cscript) registers scheduled task launching pythonw/.pyw stealer AIInstallation High
Hunts the BusySnake persistence step where a dropped VBScript registers a scheduled task that relaunches the Python stealer. Detects wscript.exe/cscript.exe as the parent of schtasks.exe /create, or a schtasks/task action referencing pythonw or a .pyw file — the exact persistence mechanism the stealer self-heals with when the task is missing. Rationale: Article: the stealer 'Ensure[s] persistence by checking if the scheduled task exists, and if not, drop[s] a VBScript to register a new scheduled task,' and runs as a .pyw (pythonw, no console). wscript-parents-schtasks and .pyw task actions are both directly named behaviors. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/armored-likho-apt-with-busysnake-stealer/120292/ • https://gbhackers.com/busysnake-stealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.005 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy logon .vbs that legitimately create scheduled tasks during login
  • Software installers using a VBScript custom action to register update tasks
  • Developer/admin registering Python jobs via pythonw for automation
  • Backup agents self-registering scheduled tasks via script wrappers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "\\Windows\\System32\\GroupPolicy\\" and ProcessCommandLine !has "OneDrive"
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the scheduled-task XML (Get-ScheduledTask / the /create args) and confirm the action points at pythonw + a .pyw in a user-writable path; correlate with the parent .vbs on disk. 2) Contain: delete the malicious task, remove the .pyw and .vbs, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: search other hosts for the same task name/pyw path and for the twin-.vbs dropper (UC1) and BusySnake C2 traffic (UC4).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pythonw",".pyw")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "cscript.exe"
    or CommandLine has_any ("pythonw",".pyw")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: VBScript-Registered Scheduled Task Launching Pythonw Stealer (BusySnake)
id: b3d7e912-4a56-4c8f-8e21-9f0a7c6b1d44
description: schtasks /create parented by wscript/cscript or referencing pythonw/.pyw, matching BusySnake self-healing persistence

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/schtasks\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\/create/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/(pythonw|\.pyw)/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe Processes.process="*/create*" (Processes.parent_process_name=wscript.exe OR Processes.parent_process_name=cscript.exe OR Processes.process="*pythonw*" OR Processes.process="*.pyw*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
BusySnake C2 beacon to Armored Likho infrastructure (named domains + IPs) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host connections to the confirmed BusySnake / Armored Likho C2 domains and IPs. High-fidelity atomic-IOC alert for the command-and-control phase; a hit means a host is beaconing to actor infrastructure regardless of the initial delivery vector. Rationale: These domains/IPs are the campaign's C2 indicators published by Kaspersky Securelist (the authoritative primary source). Note: corroboration is currently single-vendor (Kaspersky); treat as high-confidence but re-validate before hard-blocking. chickenkiller/twilightparadox are FreeDNS dynamic-DNS hosts consistent with the article's built-in-tunneling shift. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/armored-likho-apt-with-busysnake-stealer/120292/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-tool sandbox or TI enrichment appliance deliberately resolving the IOC domains
  • Analyst manually browsing to the C2 domain during investigation
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse where a benign site later occupies the same 159.198.x address
  • DNS sinkhole logging the query after a block already fired
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pythonw.exe","python.exe","ssh.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName that made the connection — pythonw.exe/ssh.exe strongly confirms BusySnake vs. a browser (possible manual/analyst). 2) Contain: block the domains/IPs at proxy+firewall, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: on the host, look back for the twin-.vbs dropper, the scheduled-task persistence, RustDesk/Go2Tunnel launch, and browser-credential staging; sweep the fleet for any other host resolving these domains.

BusySnake deploys remote-access tooling: Python stealer spawns RustDesk / Go2Tunnel reverse SSH tunnel AICommand & Control High
Hunts the post-collection stage where the Python stealer installs/starts RustDesk or opens a Go2Tunnel reverse SSH tunnel for hands-on-keyboard access. Pivot is pythonw.exe/python.exe as the parent of rustdesk.exe, ssh.exe with a -R reverse-forward flag, or a go2tunnel binary — a chain no legitimate Python job produces. Rationale: Article: C2 commands let BusySnake 'establish a reverse SSH tunnel using Go2Tunnel, install RustDesk' and its tunneling is now built into the Python code. Anchoring the remote-access binaries to a pythonw/python parent makes this near-zero-FP vs. legitimate RustDesk use. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/armored-likho-apt-with-busysnake-stealer/120292/ • https://cyberpress.org/busysnake-stealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1219 T1572 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sanctioned Python automation framework that legitimately shells out to ssh -R for a dev tunnel
  • IT deploying RustDesk via a Python-based management wrapper
  • Security researcher running go2tunnel in a lab from a Python launcher
  • CI/CD agent (python) opening reverse SSH to a build host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("\\CI\\","jenkins","gitlab-runner") and DeviceName !startswith "BUILD-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is pythonw/.pyw (not an IDE/terminal) and capture the ssh -R remote endpoint or RustDesk ID from the command line. 2) Contain: kill the tunnel/RustDesk process, block the SSH/RustDesk destination, isolate the host and reset any credentials RustDesk may have captured. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC4 C2 IOCs and the RustDesk credential-prompt screenshot exfil; search for the private key file Go2Tunnel uses and for the same reverse-SSH endpoint on other hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pythonw.exe","python.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "rustdesk.exe")
    or (FileName =~ "ssh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-R ")
    or (tolower(FileName) has "go2tunnel" or tolower(ProcessCommandLine) has "go2tunnel")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "pythonw.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "python.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "rustdesk.exe"
    or (NewProcessName endswith "ssh.exe" and CommandLine has "-R ")
    or tolower(CommandLine) has "go2tunnel"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Python Stealer Spawns RustDesk or Go2Tunnel Reverse SSH (BusySnake)
id: d5c8b1a3-9f27-4e6d-a0b4-7c2e1f9d3a66
description: pythonw/python spawning RustDesk, a go2tunnel binary, or ssh.exe -R reverse tunnel, matching BusySnake hands-on-keyboard staging
references:
  - https://securelist.com/tr/armored-likho-apt-with-busysnake-stealer/120292/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/06
tags:
  - attack.t1219
  - attack.t1572
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\pythonw.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
  rustdesk:
    Image|endswith: '\rustdesk.exe'
  go2tunnel:
    CommandLine|contains: 'go2tunnel'
  sshrev:

  condition: parent and (rustdesk or go2tunnel or sshrev)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\pythonw.exe OR *\python.exe OR *\PythonW.exe) (@Image:(*\rustdesk.exe OR *\RustDesk.exe) OR @CommandLine:(*go2tunnel* OR *Go2Tunnel*) OR (@Image:(*\ssh.exe OR *\SSH.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*-R\ *))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/python(w)?\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/rustdesk\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/go2tunnel/i OR (ImageFileName=/ssh\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/\s-R\s/)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name=pythonw.exe OR Processes.parent_process_name=python.exe) (Processes.process_name=rustdesk.exe OR Processes.process="*go2tunnel*" OR (Processes.process_name=ssh.exe AND Processes.process="*-R *")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
BusySnake credential collection: pythonw stages browser cred stores, Telegram session, and crypto-wallet JSON AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the BusySnake stealer harvesting secrets — pythonw.exe/python.exe copying or staging Chromium/Firefox credential databases (Login Data, Cookies, key4.db, logins.json), Telegram session files (tdata), and JSON cryptocurrency-wallet files. Pivot is a Python process touching these specific credential artifacts, which no benign background Python job does. Rationale: Article lists BusySnake commands to 'gather cryptocurrency wallet files with a JSON extension, collect Telegram session and credential data, and extract cookies from Mozilla Firefox and Chromium-based browsers, along with passwords.' Tying those exact artifact names to a python parent is the article-specific credential-access signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/armored-likho-apt-with-busysnake-stealer/120292/ • https://cyberpress.org/busysnake-stealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Python browser-automation/testing tool (Selenium profile copy) reading Login Data in a dev environment
  • Backup software indexing a JSON wallet-config path that happens to run under python
  • Security/DFIR tooling written in Python that inventories credential stores
  • Password-manager migration script iterating logins.json
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("selenium","playwright","pytest","\\site-packages\\selenium") and DeviceName !startswith "DEV-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the python process is pythonw/.pyw (background, no console) and not a known dev tool; check whether it subsequently connected to a UC4 C2 domain. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, and force-reset credentials/cookies for the affected browser profiles plus the user's Telegram and any crypto-wallet accounts. 3) Hunt: search for the local metadata SQLite DB and staged screenshot archive the stealer creates, and pivot the pythonw hash across the fleet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pythonw.exe","python.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","cookies.sqlite","key4.db","logins.json")
    or FolderPath has @"\Telegram Desktop\tdata\"
    or (FolderPath has_any (@"\Wallets\", @"\wallet\", @"\Ethereum\", @"\Bitcoin\") and FileName endswith ".json")
| summarize ArtifactTypes = dcount(FileName), Artifacts = make_set(FileName, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "pythonw.exe" or ActingProcessName endswith "python.exe"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","cookies.sqlite","key4.db","logins.json")
    or TargetFilePath has @"\Telegram Desktop\tdata\"
    or (TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Wallets\", @"\wallet\", @"\Ethereum\", @"\Bitcoin\") and TargetFileName endswith ".json")
| summarize ArtifactTypes = dcount(TargetFileName), Artifacts = make_set(TargetFileName, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

detection:
