osascript / Script Editor making outbound internet connection (PamStealer JXA downloader) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the PamStealer execution stage where a compiled AppleScript run in Script Editor executes a self-contained JXA downloader that stages the Rust Mach-O payload using native Objective-C networking APIs. osascript/Script Editor reaching the public internet is abnormal and maps directly to the article's payload-staging behaviour (no curl/zsh is used). Rationale: Article states the JXA downloader fetches/stages the payload via native Objective-C APIs launched from Script Editor (Cmd+R) rather than curl/zsh; osascript/Script Editor egressing to a public IP is the cleanest process-anchored pivot for that stage. Sentinel left blank because macOS osascript-initiated network events are not carried by the Windows/ASIM network tables in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/pamstealer-macos-infostealer-applescript-rust/ • https://appleinsider.com/articles/26/07/02/new-mac-infostealer-confirms-stolen-passwords-before-stealing-data
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.002 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin AppleScript/JXA automation that calls a web API or Slack/Jira webhook
  • MDM or Jamf self-service scripts using osascript to fetch config
  • Developer testing a JXA script that downloads a resource
  • Backup/sync utilities that shell through osascript to an update endpoint
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith "slack.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith "jamfcloud.com" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "/Library/Application Support/JAMF"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the remote host; determine if the destination is a known-good API or an unfamiliar IP/domain, and whether a Mach-O was written to Downloads/tmp immediately after. 2. Contain: isolate the host and kill the osascript/Script Editor process tree if the destination is unknown or resolves to avenger-sync.live infrastructure. 3. Hunt: look on the same host for a Finder-named binary executing from a non-/System path and new login-item plists created shortly after the connection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("osascript","Script Editor")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort

PamStealer encrypted exfiltration to avenger-sync[.]live AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound connections to the PamStealer command-and-control / exfiltration endpoint avenger-sync[.]live, to which the Rust second stage sends encrypted browser data, wallet data, iCloud Keychain secrets and the captured login password over HTTP. This is a hardcoded C2 IOC corroborated across sources. Rationale: avenger-sync[.]live is the confirmed exfiltration endpoint (Jamf notes it aligns with the avngr/avenger delivery infrastructure across the sample set); a resolution or connection is a strong post-collection actions-on-objective signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/pamstealer-macos-infostealer-applescript-rust/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/pamstealer-uses-fake-maccy-sites-and.html

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Analyst manually resolving the IOC during investigation
  • Passive-DNS or scanning service in the org resolving the domain
  • Blocklist-validation tooling checking that the domain is sinkholed
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("soc-sandbox-mac","malware-analysis-vm")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm which process on the host connected to avenger-sync.live and whether it is a Finder-masquerading Mach-O; treat any user endpoint hit as a confirmed compromise given collection has already occurred. 2. Contain: isolate the host, block avenger-sync.live and the maccyapp.* domains, and force-reset the user's macOS login password plus any credentials/cookies/wallets that were resident (browser saved passwords, iCloud Keychain, crypto wallets). 3. Hunt: enumerate other hosts resolving avenger-sync.live or the maccyapp.* domains and check for the Finder/System Settings masquerade and login-item persistence.

Finder or System Settings Mach-O executing from non-system path (PamStealer masquerade) AIInstallation High
Hunts the PamStealer second stage, a Rust arm64 Mach-O that masquerades as Finder.app, and the bundled helper that impersonates System Settings for persistence. Legitimate Finder and System Settings only execute from under /System/, so a process with those names running from a user-writable path is a direct masquerade hit. Rationale: Article and Jamf confirm the Rust second stage masquerades as Finder.app and a bundled arm64 Mach-O impersonates System Settings; the legitimate binaries live only under /System/Library/CoreServices and /System/Applications, so name-match plus non-/System path is high-fidelity with negligible legitimate overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/pamstealer-macos-infostealer-applescript-rust/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/pamstealer-uses-fake-maccy-sites-and.html
ATT&CKT1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer building a project whose output binary happens to be named 'Finder' running from a build/DerivedData path
  • QA harness copying System Settings.app to a staging path for automation
  • Backup restore staging an app bundle to /Users/Shared before moving it
  • A renamed diagnostic tool coincidentally named 'Finder' in a user home directory
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !startswith "/Applications/" and FolderPath !has "/DerivedData/" and FolderPath !has "/Xcode/"
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the FolderPath, SHA256 and parent process; verify the binary is not code-signed by Apple and check the path (Downloads, /tmp, /var/folders, ~/Library indicate malware). 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and quarantine the Mach-O; block avenger-sync.live and the maccyapp.* domains. 3. Hunt: on the same host look for the osascript JXA download that preceded it, new LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plists, and SMAppService login-item registration; sweep the fleet for the same SHA256.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("Finder","System Settings")
| where FolderPath !startswith "/System/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/Finder" or TargetProcessName endswith "/System Settings"
| where not(TargetProcessName startswith "/System/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)`
| where NOT match(process_path,"^/System/")
| sort - lastTime
Login-item persistence plist written by non-Apple process (PamStealer SMAppService/legacy) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts PamStealer's persistence: the Rust stage registers its Finder-masquerading bundle as a login item both via the modern SMAppService API and via a helper written to /tmp that adds a legacy login item. This surfaces LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist creation authored by a process running outside Apple/system paths. Rationale: Jamf confirms PamStealer persists by registering its Finder bundle as a login item via SMAppService and via a /tmp helper that writes a legacy login item; scoping plist creation in LaunchAgents/LaunchDaemons to non-Apple authoring processes captures that without alerting on Apple/installer-managed persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/pamstealer-macos-infostealer-applescript-rust/ • https://appleinsider.com/articles/26/07/02/new-mac-infostealer-confirms-stolen-passwords-before-stealing-data
ATT&CKT1547.015 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate third-party app (Dropbox, Zoom, Docker) installing its own LaunchAgent on first run
  • Homebrew services writing a LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist
  • Jamf/MDM deploying a managed LaunchDaemon
  • A developer's build script installing a helper daemon during testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Dropbox","zoom.us","Docker","brew","jamf") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/Applications/"
Response runbook
1. Triage: read the created plist's ProgramArguments and the authoring process path; a plist pointing at a Finder/System Settings binary in Downloads, /tmp or ~/Library is malicious. 2. Contain: isolate the host, unload and delete the offending plist, remove the login item, and quarantine the referenced Mach-O. 3. Hunt: correlate with the preceding osascript network egress and Finder-masquerade execution on the same host, and sweep the fleet for identical plist ProgramArguments or the same referenced binary hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".plist"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/System/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/usr/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/Library/Apple/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".plist"
| where not(ActingProcessName startswith "/System/") and not(ActingProcessName startswith "/usr/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Installation
Detected
Phase 6
Command & Control
Likely
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — How We Added WebAuthn to a Browser-Based RDP Client
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub Actions runner outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com (tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts a self-hosted CI/CD runner process (Runner.Worker/node/python/curl) reaching gist.githubusercontent.com — the exact egress the compromised tj-actions/changed-files action used to pull its memory-dumping Python second stage. This was StepSecurity Harden-Runner's original detection signal for the March 2025 incident. Rationale: Uses the corroborated network IOC (outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com from a runner) that StepSecurity's Harden-Runner used to detect CVE-2025-30066; scoped to runner process ancestry (Runner.Worker/node/python/_actions paths) to separate it from ordinary developer gist fetches. Cross-checked against CISA, Wiz and Sysdig write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build step legitimately curls a config/install script hosted on a GitHub gist
  • Developer tooling or dotfiles bootstrap that pulls from gist.githubusercontent.com on a self-hosted runner
  • Package post-install hooks fetching helper scripts from a gist
  • Security tooling / EDR test harness deliberately reaching gist domains
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation resolving raw gist content
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("renovate","dependabot") or RemoteUrl has "raw.githubusercontent.com/your-org")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and parent chain of the initiating process; confirm it ran inside a GitHub Actions job (Runner.Worker/_work/_actions path) and identify the workflow/repo. Grab the exact gist URL and the resolved IP. 2) Contain: if the job used tj-actions/changed-files (or any action pinned to a mutable tag), pause the runner, and immediately rotate every secret exposed to workflows that ran between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC (access keys, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, RSA keys). 3) Hunt: search the same runner fleet for the malicious commit 0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67 and for double-base64 blobs written to workflow logs; review runner egress for other first-seen domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or RemoteUrl has "gist.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","python.exe","python3","python","curl.exe","curl","wget","Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker")
     or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker","node.exe","node")
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("actions-runner","_work","_actions")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or HttpHostName in~ ("gist.githubusercontent.com","gist.github.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

tj-actions/changed-files malicious commit 0e58ed86 referenced on host (CVE-2025-30066) AIDelivery High
Alerts on the exact malicious tj-actions/changed-files commit SHA (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67) appearing in any process command line or file path on a self-hosted runner — i.e. the compromised action being fetched, checked out, or pinned. A pure, second-source-confirmed IOC hunt for the retagged supply-chain payload. Rationale: Uses the article's SHA1 (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67), independently confirmed by CISA and the GitHub Advisory as the single malicious commit every tj-actions/changed-files tag (v1.0.0–v44.5.1) was pointed to — a unique, zero-ambiguity IOC that only appears when the compromised action is fetched, checked out, or SHA-pinned. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-mrrh-fwg8-r2c3 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/github-actions-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/threat-intel tooling scanning for the hash as an IOC (grep, EDR IOC sweep) surfaces the string in its own command line
  • A remediation script that greps repos/workflows for the malicious SHA
  • Vulnerability-management agent enumerating the commit as data
  • A security researcher reproducing/analyzing the incident in a lab runner
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("grep.exe","findstr.exe","rg.exe","select-string") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("IOC","threat-intel","scan-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA appears in a real action fetch/checkout (Runner.Worker/git/_actions context) versus an analyst's own IOC-scan process; identify the repo and the workflow run time. 2) Contain: treat the runner and any workflow that executed the action as compromised — rotate all secrets exposed to workflows run between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC, and repin tj-actions/changed-files to the patched v46.0.1 by full SHA. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound gist.githubusercontent.com egress from the same runner, inspect workflow logs for double-base64 secret blobs, and check for the sibling reviewdog/action-setup CVE-2025-30154 across the fleet.
let ioc = "0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67";
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has ioc or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ioc
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ProcessEvent", Account=AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine, Context=InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
 (DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where FolderPath has ioc or FileName has ioc or FolderPath has "tj-actions/changed-files"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="FileEvent", Account=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Evidence=FolderPath, Context=InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Process memory read via /proc/<pid>/mem targeting GitHub Actions Runner.Worker (TeamPCP Trivy stealer) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the TeamPCP credential-stealer's core collection step: a payload process reading /proc/<numeric-pid>/mem to scrape marked secrets ({"value":...,"isSecret":true}) out of the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process memory. The numeric-PID regex excludes benign /proc/self/mem access, making cross-process memory reads on a CI runner a high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's literal code block `/proc/pid/mem` and the Runner.Worker target; the numeric-PID regex is the discriminator (legit /proc/self/mem is excluded). Aqua's GHSA advisory and Microsoft's guidance both confirm the stealer reads /proc/<pid>/mem from Runner.Worker searching for {"value":...,"isSecret":true}. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/24/detecting-investigating-defending-against-trivy-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/from-scanner-to-stealer-inside-the-trivy-action-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/SRE running gdb or gcore to capture a core dump during CI debugging
  • Memory-forensics tooling (AVML, LiME, volatility helpers) invoked in an incident-response pipeline
  • Performance profilers (perf, valgrind, heaptrack) attaching to a target PID
  • Language-runtime crash handlers that snapshot another process's memory
  • Container runtime health/introspection tools reading /proc/<pid>/mem of a monitored child
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("gdb","lldb","valgrind","criu","gcore","perf","heaptrack")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain — confirm the reader is a runner-spawned interpreter (python/node/sh) and the target PID resolves to Runner.Worker, not a debugger the dev launched. Check the runner's checked-out action refs for aquasecurity/trivy-action or setup-trivy. 2) Contain: cancel/isolate the CI job, revoke the runner's GITHUB_TOKEN and any cloud creds (AWS/GCP/Azure), and rotate every secret the workflow could read — assume exposure. 3) Hunt: pivot to that host's egress for scan.aquasecurtiy.org / 45.148.10.212 and to any process referencing 'tpcp-docs'; sweep all repos for the compromised action tags.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName !in~ ("gdb","lldb","valgrind","criu","gcore","perf")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
     or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| where TargetProcessName !in~ ("gdb","lldb","valgrind","criu","gcore","perf")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exfiltration to TeamPCP typosquat C2 scan.aquasecurtiy.org / stealer IPs from CI runner AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the TeamPCP stealer's primary exfil: an HTTPS POST of AES/RSA-wrapped secrets to the typosquat domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org (mimics aquasecurity.com) resolving to 45.148.10.212, plus the campaign's additional stealer IPs. Any connection to this fixed attacker infrastructure is a confirmed compromise. Rationale: Uses the exact typosquat domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org and IP 45.148.10.212 named in the article body, plus the two campaign IPs from the IOC bundle. Aqua GHSA, Wiz and CrowdStrike all confirm scan.aquasecurtiy.org → 45.148.10.212 as the primary HTTPS-POST exfil channel. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 • https://www.wiz.io/blog/trivy-compromised-teampcp-supply-chain-attack • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/teampcp-supply-chain-attack-campaign-targets-trivy-checkmarx-kics-and-litellm-potential-downstream-impact-to-additional-projects/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An analyst or sandbox intentionally detonating the sample and beaconing to the C2 during research
  • A DNS-sinkhole or threat-intel scanner that resolves/probes the typosquat domain for tracking
  • IOC-validation tooling that curls the domain to confirm takedown status
  • Threat-hunt reproduction traffic generated during tabletop exercises
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host/runner and the InitiatingProcess that opened the socket; confirm it is a CI job using a compromised trivy-action/setup-trivy or KICS tag. Because payloads are AES-256+RSA-4096 wrapped, do not rely on packet inspection — the destination alone is the verdict. 2) Contain: block the domain and all three IPs at the egress proxy/firewall, kill the job, and immediately rotate every secret reachable by that workflow (GITHUB_TOKEN, cloud keys, registry creds). 3) Hunt: search all runners for /proc/<pid>/mem reads (UC1) and for the 'tpcp-docs' fallback (UC4), and enumerate every repo referencing the poisoned actions.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl =~ "scan.aquasecurtiy.org"
     or RemoteIP in ("45.148.10.212","83.142.209.203","94.154.172.43")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("45.148.10.212","83.142.209.203","94.154.172.43")
     or DestinationHostName =~ "scan.aquasecurtiy.org"
     or RequestURL has "scan.aquasecurtiy.org"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP,
          DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationPort, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Org-wide DNS lookups to TeamPCP campaign domains (Trivy / Checkmarx KICS / LiteLLM) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution of the full TeamPCP campaign domain set spanning the Trivy exfil host, the Checkmarx KICS lures (checkmarx.zone, audit.checkmarx.cx), the LiteLLM PyPI stealer C2 (models.litellm.cloud), and the Internet Computer canister fallback. Distinct from the runner-egress detection: this is an org-wide DNS pivot that catches any host touched by any arm of the campaign. Rationale: Combines the article's exfil domain with the pre-extracted campaign IOC domains (checkmarx.zone, audit.checkmarx.cx, models.litellm.cloud, and the full ICP canister host). Arctic Wolf and Kaspersky both attribute the Checkmarx-KICS and LiteLLM PyPI stealers to the same TeamPCP actor, so a hit on any of these is campaign-linked. Datadog left empty — the provided linux sources expose no DNS-question field. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/teampcp-supply-chain-attack-campaign-targets-trivy-checkmarx-kics-and-litellm-potential-downstream-impact-to-additional-projects/ • https://www.kaspersky.com/blog/critical-supply-chain-attack-trivy-litellm-checkmarx-teampcp/55510/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment platforms resolving the IOC domains for tracking/takedown monitoring
  • Security researchers detonating campaign samples in a lab that shares DNS telemetry
  • A legitimate developer typo'ing aquasecurity.com and hitting the typosquat once (single, non-repeating query)
  • Passive-DNS or brand-protection scanners crawling the typosquat namespace
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which host/user resolved the domain and the initiating process; determine which campaign arm it maps to (Trivy runner, Checkmarx KICS, or a LiteLLM/PyPI install). 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domain org-wide, isolate the resolving host, and rotate credentials that host or its pipelines could reach. 3) Hunt: for CI hosts pivot to UC1 (/proc/mem) and UC4 (tpcp-docs); for developer endpoints, inspect recent pip installs of litellm/telnyx and Python process ancestry for the stealer.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("scan.aquasecurtiy.org","checkmarx.zone","audit.checkmarx.cx","models.litellm.cloud","tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub-native fallback exfil: creation of public 'tpcp-docs' repo by TeamPCP stealer AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the stealer's fallback exfil channel documented by second sources: when scan.aquasecurtiy.org is unreachable and INPUT_GITHUB_PAT is present, the payload creates a public repo named tpcp-docs and uploads stolen data as release assets. Any process on a runner referencing 'tpcp-docs' (via git/gh/curl to api.github.com) is a unique, high-fidelity attacker artifact. Rationale: The unique attacker artifact 'tpcp-docs' (public repo name for the GitHub-native fallback exfil) has near-zero benign collision. Not in the article body but confirmed by Aqua's GHSA advisory, Microsoft's detection guidance ("look for public repositories named tpcp-docs"), and NVD remediation notes — so it is corroborated by multiple second sources and shipped accordingly. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/24/detecting-investigating-defending-against-trivy-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/trivy-compromised-teampcp-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A responder or researcher naming a scratch/IOC repo 'tpcp-docs' while investigating this campaign
  • A takedown/monitoring script that references the attacker repo name to check for its existence
  • Internal detection-engineering test harnesses that seed the string 'tpcp-docs' to validate this rule
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and parent process; confirm it is a git/gh/curl invocation creating or pushing to a public repo named tpcp-docs from a CI runner. Query the org's GitHub for any repo named tpcp-docs and delete/quarantine. 2) Contain: revoke the runner's GITHUB_TOKEN and any PAT (INPUT_GITHUB_PAT) exposed to the job, delete the attacker repo and its release assets, and rotate all reachable secrets. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (/proc/mem read) and UC2/UC3 (C2 egress) on the same host, and audit all workflows using aquasecurity/trivy-action, aquasecurity/setup-trivy, and Checkmarx KICS during the Mar 19–22 window.

| where ProcessCommandLine has "tpcp-docs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] 9router API key / secret exfiltration via /api/settings/database without prior login
9router API key / secret exfiltration via /api/settings/database without prior login AIActions on Objectives Medium
After forging a session cookie, the attacker reads stored provider API keys and auth tokens from 9router's /api/settings/database endpoint. This correlates access to the settings/secret endpoints against the source ever having performed a successful POST /api/auth/login — a forged-token holder never logs in, so absence of a login is the tell. Rationale: Targets the article's named exfiltration path /api/settings/database ("steal valuable API Key, Auth Token") and the operational fact that a forged cookie bypasses the login flow entirely — so a leftanti against successful POST /api/auth/login isolates forged sessions. Sigma/Datadog/Defender/Falcon empty: this is a multi-event correlation on web-tier logs, not a single-event or endpoint signal. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/CVE-2026-49352/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jphh-m39h-6gwx
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin session where the login POST landed outside the lookback window or was logged by a different proxy node (login not observed for that src)
  • Automation / IaC that reads 9router settings using a long-lived valid cookie and never re-authenticates in-window
  • Shared NAT egress where one user logged in and another admin IP-shares the same source address
  • Health-check or config-backup jobs polling /api/settings
Suppression filter
// Exclude known automation egress IPs that legitimately read settings with a persistent session:
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.20.0.15", "10.20.0.16")   // replace with your config-management egress IPs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full request sequence for the SrcIpAddr; confirm the auth_token cookie matches the forged shape from UC1 and that no successful /api/auth/login exists for it across all proxy nodes. Check HTTP status on /api/settings/database (200 = secrets returned). 2) CONTAIN: Rotate ALL provider API keys and auth tokens held by 9router immediately (treat as disclosed), set JWT_SECRET + restart, block the source IP. 3) HUNT: Check for password-change and shutdown API calls from the same source, and for outbound use of the stolen keys against upstream provider APIs (billing/usage spikes).
let Lookback = 7d;
let LoggedIn = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where HttpMethod == "POST"
    | where Url has "/api/auth/login"
    | where HttpStatusCode between (200 .. 299)
    | distinct SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where Url has "/api/settings/database" or Url has "/api/settings"
| where HttpRequestHeaderCookie has "auth_token="
| where SrcIpAddr !in (LoggedIn)     // forged-token holder never authenticated
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderCookie
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/settings/database*" OR Web.uri_path="*/api/settings*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.uri_path Web.http_method Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| join type=left src [ | tstats `summariesonly` count as login_count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*/api/auth/login*" Web.http_method=POST (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=204) by Web.src | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` ]
| where isnull(login_count)
| sort - lastTime
| table firstTime lastTime src dest uri_path http_method status
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/settings/database*" OR Web.uri_path="*/api/settings*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.uri_path Web.http_method Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| join type=left src [ | tstats summariesonly=false count as login_count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*/api/auth/login*" Web.http_method=POST (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=204) by Web.src | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` ]
| where isnull(login_count)
| sort - lastTime
| table firstTime lastTime src dest uri_path http_method status
9router unauthenticated MCP / cli-tools route RCE via process spawn — CVE-2026-46339 AIExploitation Medium
The 9router middleware only guards 8 routes, leaving /api/mcp/* and /api/cli-tools/* (40+ routes, added in v0.4.30) with no authentication, allowing unauthenticated OS command execution as the 9router user. Detects both the inbound requests to those routes and the resulting node process spawning a shell/interpreter child on the host. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable route prefixes named in the CVE-2026-46339 write-up (/api/mcp/*, /api/cli-tools/*, unguarded since v0.4.30) for the web tier, and the RCE's on-host signature (the node process spawning a shell) for EDR. Corroborated via the GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj advisory and Endor Labs' analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj • https://www.endorlabs.com/vulnerability/cve-2026-46339
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate authorized use of the 9router MCP stdio->SSE bridge invoking a local tool that spawns a helper process
  • node-based build tooling / npm scripts on a shared dev box spawning sh/bash (scope the EDR rule to the 9router server to remove this)
  • MCP plugin health-checks or self-tests that shell out
  • Monitoring agents that proxy /api/mcp/ readiness probes
Suppression filter
// EDR side: scope to the 9router install path once known, to strip generic node->shell dev noise:
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("9router", "node_modules\\9router")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Correlate the /api/mcp/ or /api/cli-tools/ request time against the node->shell spawn on the same host; inspect ProcessCommandLine / InitiatingProcessCommandLine for attacker commands (whoami, curl, base64, reverse-shell). Confirm 9router version is 0.4.30-0.4.36 (unpatched for CVE-2026-46339). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, upgrade 9router to >=0.4.45, and restrict /api/mcp/ + /api/cli-tools/ at the proxy/WAF. 3) HUNT: Sweep for persistence and outbound C2 from the node process (DeviceNetworkEvents / NetworkConnectIP4 with ContextImageFileName node), dropped files, and reuse of the same source IP against other exposed 9router hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/mcp/" or Url has "/api/cli-tools/"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderCookie
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GravitLauncher LaunchServer secret read via unauth path traversal (ecdsa_id/legacySalt/LaunchServer.json) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to the LaunchServer file server that reference the server's own secret files outside updatesDir (.keys/ecdsa_id, .keys/rsa_id, .keys/legacySalt, LaunchServer.json). A successful read of ecdsa_id hands the attacker the JWT signing key, yielding a full admin auth bypass, so any such request is high-fidelity regardless of traversal encoding. Rationale: Uses the exact secret filenames the advisory names as readable outside updatesDir (.keys/ecdsa_id, rsa_id, legacySalt, LaunchServer.json) — legitimate GravitLauncher clients only fetch update payloads under updatesDir and never reference these, so any hit is near-certainly exploitation of CVE-2026-54617. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5g75-477j-2c2f • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/pro.gravit.launcher/launchserver-api/CVE-2026-54617/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Nuclei) running a CVE-2026-54617 template against the LaunchServer host
  • Internal red-team / pentest engagement replaying the PoC
  • An update artifact legitimately named LaunchServer.json placed inside updatesDir and requested by a client
  • Security researcher probing the public 9274 endpoint after the CVE disclosure
  • Backup/monitoring tooling misconfigured to fetch config files over the file-server port
Suppression filter
| where DeviceProduct != "VulnScanner" and SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0")  // exclude the sanctioned scanner subnet / host once identified
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request line and HTTP status for the source IP — a 200/OK with a non-zero body means the secret bytes were actually served (compromise); a 404 means the safe leading-slash branch was hit. Note whether the target was ecdsa_id/legacySalt (auth bypass) or LaunchServer.json (DB creds). 2) Contain: firewall port 9274 to internal only or rebind LaunchServer to 127.0.0.1; treat the ECDSA signing key, legacySalt and DB credentials as compromised and rotate all three immediately, invalidating outstanding JWTs. 3) Hunt: from the same source IP look for follow-on `../../../../etc/passwd`-style reads, and pivot to authentication logs for anomalous admin-account token use or DB logins from new IPs after the read timestamp.
let LaunchServerSecrets = dynamic(["ecdsa_id","rsa_id",".keys","legacySalt","LaunchServer.json"]);

| where RequestURL has_any (LaunchServerSecrets)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

LaunchServer path-traversal exploit signature: request-target without leading slash / %2e%2e on port 9274 AIExploitation High
Hunts the structural exploitation signature of CVE-2026-54617 — an HTTP request-target that does NOT begin with '/' (e.g. 'GET ../../.keys/ecdsa_id') or uses '%2e%2e' encoding, aimed at the default 0.0.0.0:9274 file-server bind. This catches depth-robust arbitrary-file reads (../../../../etc/passwd) that the secret-filename query would miss, since only the no-leading-slash form escapes updatesDir. Rationale: Keys on the advisory's unique root-cause signature: only a request-target lacking a leading slash (or %2e%2e-encoded) escapes updatesDir, while curl/browsers/normal clients always prepend '/'. Port 9274 is the article's default 0.0.0.0 bind; the Defender/Falcon clauses only give coarse public-inbound-to-9274 exposure because FDR/AH carry no HTTP URI. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5g75-477j-2c2f • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/pro.gravit.launcher/launchserver-api/CVE-2026-54617/
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanner firing generic '../' and '%2e%2e' path-traversal payloads at the endpoint
  • Misbehaving HTTP client or crawler emitting a relative (non-absolute) request-target
  • Legitimate query-string parameter that happens to contain '../' being logged in RequestURL
  • Load-balancer / L4 health-check tooling hitting 9274 with non-standard request lines
  • Defender/Falcon exposure clause alone: any benign public connection to 9274 (this clause is exposure, not exploitation)
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL has "../" and RequestURL !startswith ".." and RequestURL !has "%2e%2e")  // keep only the no-leading-slash / encoded form, drop benign embedded ../ in query strings
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request-target genuinely lacks a leading slash or uses %2e%2e (the exploit form) versus a normal '/..' that the server 404s; check the HTTP status and byte count to see if a file was served. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the L4 firewall and restrict 9274 to trusted management ranges or rebind to 127.0.0.1; a normalizing L7 proxy in front returns 400 for these — deploy or enforce one. 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct traversal target from that IP (etc/passwd, .keys/*, LaunchServer.json) to gauge what was read, and if any secret was served, rotate the ECDSA key/legacySalt/DB creds and audit downstream JWT and DB activity.

fast-mcp-telegram traversal token in request URL (URL-auth middleware) CVE-2026-52830 AIExploitation High
Hunts the URL-auth variant of CVE-2026-52830 where the traversal token is carried in the request path/query rather than the Authorization header. Surfaces web access-log requests to a fast-mcp-telegram server whose URI contains '../fast-mcp-telegram/telegram', %2e%2e-encoded traversal, or a direct telegram.session reference. Rationale: Pivots on the URL field instead of the Authorization header (the article calls out both header auth and URL auth, and URL-encoded traversal 'if any route decodes path components'), using the same concrete CVE strings so it catches deployments that log full URIs but strip auth headers. Distinct log field and platform coverage (CIM Web/W3CIISLog) from the header UC. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52830 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/fast-mcp-telegram/CVE-2026-52830/

Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Legitimate URLs whose query string happens to contain %2e%2e from over-encoding
  • Authorized pentest replaying the URL-auth bypass

| where status < 300 AND NOT match(http_user_agent, "(?i)(nuclei|zap|burp|nmap|acunetix)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the URI targeted a real fast-mcp-telegram route and resolved to the telegram.session file (token '../fast-mcp-telegram/telegram' or %2e%2e variant); check the response status to tell an accepted bypass (2xx) from a rejected probe. 2) Contain: block the source at the WAF, patch to fast-mcp-telegram >=0.19.1, and invalidate/rotate the default telegram.session and its Telegram login. 3) Hunt: correlate the SrcIpAddr to subsequent MCP tool invocations and to the Authorization-header UC; enumerate other traversal encodings (Windows separators, absolute paths, double-URL-encoding) and confirm no messages were sent from the default account during the exposure window.

9router node process spawns 'sudo -S sh' (GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p command-injection primitive) AIExploitation High
Hunts the OS command-injection primitive in 9router's /api/tunnel/tailscale-install route: the Node.js server (or the '9router' binary) spawning 'sudo -S sh', whose stdin is fed the attacker-controlled sudoPassword field as a shell command. A long-running web server spawning an interactive privileged shell is the article-specific tell of exploitation (or of the rarely-used legitimate Tailscale install). Rationale: Anchors on the exact spawn from the advisory's tailscale.js:304-341 — spawn("sudo", ["-S", "sh"]) with parent node/9router. This process shape is emitted on every invocation of the vulnerable route, so it catches both successful root RCE and the process even when sudo later rejects the payload. Corroborated by GitLab GLAD and vendor repo decolua/9router. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/ • https://github.com/decolua/9router/security • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1548.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate operator installs Tailscale through the 9router dashboard's 'Install Tailscale' button (identical process chain)
  • Other Node automation tooling on the host that shells out via sudo -S to run privileged install scripts
  • A configuration-management agent written in Node (e.g. a custom deploy daemon) invoking sudo -S sh
  • Developer laptop where 9router is run interactively and Tailscale is genuinely being installed
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessId != prev(InitiatingProcessId)  // dedup per server session; correlate with an unauthenticated/external source IP on /api/tunnel/tailscale-install before escalating
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ProcessCommandLine of the child 'sh' and its subsequent children on the same host/session — the injected sudoPassword becomes the first shell command (look for 'id', file writes to /tmp, curl|wget, reverse-shell one-liners, or a trailing '; exit 0'). Confirm the parent node process is the 9router server and check whether it runs as uid 0. 2) Contain: isolate the host/container; if it is a container running as root, stop it and rebuild from an image that adds a non-root USER; rotate any secrets reachable from the process. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP that hit /api/tunnel/tailscale-install (web/proxy logs), and search other 9router hosts for the same node->sudo -S sh chain and for the sibling node->curl tailscale.com/install.sh event. Upgrade all 9router instances to >=0.4.45.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "sudo"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("-S", "sh")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "9router")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessId, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "sudo"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("-S", "sh")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node", "9router")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router node process fetches tailscale.com/install.sh via curl (vulnerable route invoked) AIDelivery High
Hunts the download step of 9router's /api/tunnel/tailscale-install handler: the Node.js server spawning 'curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh'. Per the advisory's impact table this outbound fetch fires on EVERY invocation of the unauthenticated route — including cases where sudo later rejects the payload and no RCE occurs — making it the most reliable host-side marker that the vulnerable endpoint was reached. Rationale: Uses the exact command from tailscale.js: spawn("curl", ["-fsSL", "https://tailscale.com/install.sh"]) with parent node/9router. Because the advisory confirms this fetch happens even in the non-root 'no RCE' case, it is a lower-severity but higher-recall companion to the sudo -S sh detection. Corroborated by GitLab GLAD and vendor repo. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/ • https://github.com/decolua/9router/security
ATT&CKT1190 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator legitimately installing Tailscale from the 9router dashboard
  • Admin manually running the official Tailscale install command from a shell that happens to have a node-named parent
  • CI pipeline step that provisions Tailscale on a build agent via curl | sh
  • Container entrypoint that installs Tailscale at startup
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is the 9router/node server and check for a following node->sudo -S sh event on the same host within seconds; review web/proxy logs for a POST to /api/tunnel/tailscale-install and whether it carried auth cookies or came from an external IP. 2) Contain: if the source was unauthenticated/external, isolate the host/container and treat as active exploitation; block the source IP at the edge. 3) Hunt: sweep all 9router hosts for this curl chain and for the sudo -S sh primitive; verify version and upgrade to >=0.4.45, and ensure the container runs as a non-root USER.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "curl"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "tailscale.com/install.sh"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "9router")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "curl"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "tailscale.com/install.sh"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node", "9router")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated POST to 9router /api/tunnel/tailscale-install endpoint AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP access-log evidence of the 9router RCE (GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p): a POST to /api/tunnel/tailscale-install, the unauthenticated spawn-capable route that bypasses dashboardGuard. Valuable for Dockerised deployments without endpoint EDR, where the reverse-proxy / app HTTP log is the only visibility into the attack. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable route path and method from the advisory (POST /api/tunnel/tailscale-install). Web-log visibility is the fallback pivot for root-Docker deployments that lack endpoint EDR; the request path is unique enough that any external hit warrants triage. Corroborated by GitLab GLAD and the related fix (CVE-2026-46339) that gated /api/tunnel/* to loopback. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator clicking 'Install Tailscale' in the 9router dashboard (legitimate POST to the same path)
  • Internal vulnerability scanner or ASM tool probing the endpoint
  • Health-check or synthetic monitor configured against tunnel routes
  • Loopback (127.0.0.1) requests from the patched local-only gate after upgrade to >=0.4.45
Suppression filter
| where CIp !startswith "127." and CIp != "::1"  // exclude the patched loopback-only path and local dashboard use
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the source IP (CIp) — loopback/internal-dashboard vs external/unexpected — and whether the deployment is patched (>=0.4.45, which restricts /api/tunnel/* to loopback). Correlate with host process telemetry for node->curl tailscale.com/install.sh and node->sudo -S sh in the same time window. 2) Contain: if the request is external/unauthenticated, block the source IP at the edge and isolate the affected host/container. 3) Hunt: enumerate all internet-facing 9router instances, confirm they are not running as root and are upgraded; review earlier requests from the same IP for reconnaissance of other spawn-capable routes (/api/mcp/*, /api/cli-tools/*).

| where CsUriStem =~ "/api/tunnel/tailscale-install"
| project TimeGenerated, CIp, CsMethod, CsUriStem, ScStatus, TimeTaken, UserAgent, CsHost
| order by TimeGenerated desc
